title: NICER 2021 data show that deep soft X-ray suppression in ASASSN-14ko keeps a 108.46-day period and a 5.5-day lead on the UV peak in 2020-2024, while the dip onset moves by up to 6 days
abstract: Question: a Swift XRT clock found that the soft X-ray dips of the repeating nuclear transient ASASSN-14ko repeat at a constant 108.44 d in 2020-2024, so the published period decrease stopped. That clock had no dip in 2021-2022 and used one marker definition. Approach: we reduced all 163 public NICER observations (2020-2023, 413 ks) without HEASoft, with an empirical background model calibrated and validated on 139 NICER blank-sky observations. We froze the predictions of nine published ephemerides for cycles 21-25 before fitting, then measured the dip time of every cycle (NICER and XRT combined) with four definitions and tested ephemerides and a random-walk period-kick model. Results: the 2021 dips start to fall 1-6 d before the deep suppression, so onset markers move by up to 6 d and need 0.85-2.2 d of jitter. The time of deep suppression (first crossing of 30 percent of the pre-dip rate) fits one period of 108.46 d with no excess jitter in eight cycles (residuals below 0.6 d, except a poorly sampled cycle), Pdot -0.0006 to +0.0009 (95 percent), and stays -5.50 +/- 0.36 d before the UVW2 peak in seven cycles (chi2 2.4 for 6 dof). All four markers reject the published Pdot = -0.0026 (delta chi2 14.6-26.1, jitter free). The NICER-era dips cannot separate the frozen stall models (differences up to 3 d); only a constant-Pdot fit is disfavoured for small jitter. For the deep-suppression marker, period kicks are below 0.35-0.6 d per orbit (95 percent), which disfavours the 0.6-0.9 d fitted to optical peaks. Limitations: we chose the 30 percent marker after inspecting the light curves; the kick limit and constant lag depend on it, the Pdot rejection does not; the background model is empirical; no X-ray data exist after 2024 July.

display.caption: Soft X-ray dips of eight ASASSN-14ko flares from NICER (blue) and Swift XRT (red), aligned on the linear 108.437-d X-ray clock. Green and orange bands: 30 and 50 percent crossing times (68 percent). The 2021 dips start to fall days before the deep suppression, which stays on the clock.

Top: four X-ray dip markers minus the linear clock, with the best fit that uses the Payne et al. Pdot and three frozen predictions. Bottom: marker minus UVW2 peak. The 30 percent crossing stays on one period and keeps a constant 5.5-d lead; the onset markers do not.

Left and middle: validation of the empirical NICER background model on 139 blank-sky observations. Right: likelihood profile of random period kicks for the four marker sets; the deep-suppression marker disfavours kicks of 0.6-0.9 d per orbit.

citations.reason: We use its XRT light curves, box-ingress and UVW2 posteriors and linear clock. NICER adds 2021 dips; the deep-suppression time confirms its constant period and 5.5-d lag, but its box ingress is shape dependent for gradual dips.
We froze its clock-model predictions for the NICER cycles. Only its constant-Pdot fit M0 is disfavoured, and only for small jitter; the stall models cannot be separated there.
We use its Swift UVOT UVW2 per-visit photometry in Figure 1.
Its random period kicks of about 0.6 d per orbit are disfavoured by the deep-suppression X-ray clock, if that marker is the orbital clock.
Its period noise beyond a cubic trend is not seen in the deep-suppression X-ray times of 2020-2024 (marker-dependent result).
Its constant period near 108 d after 2020 agrees with our X-ray clock of 108.46 d in 2020-2024.
A changing UV emission delay after the debris arrives is excluded by the constant lag of deep suppression to the UV peak in seven cycles.
Its wider optical rises after 2021 agree with the more gradual X-ray dip onsets that NICER shows in 2021.
Later SPHEREx timing that the X-ray clock does not cover.
Payne et al. ephemeris with Pdot = -0.0026; rejected by all four X-ray dip markers in 2020-2024. Also the first NICER reduction of 2020-2021.
